UPDATE: GEKCO SLAPP suit

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The biggest SLAPP suit in South African history has been withdrawn.

Unique Selling Point:
In 2021, we reported on the R197 million suit that Century Property Developments had brought against the Greater Kyalami Conservany (GEKCO) and its chair, Kristin Kallesen. In January this year, that suit was withdrawn.

Summary:
GEKCO is a conservation organisation working outside Johannesburg's northern boundary - which also happens to be one of the most rapidly developing areas in South Africa. The developments are mostly under Century, which is building commercial zones and housing such as Riversands Commercial Park and Helderfontein residential estate. In 2021, GEKCO lodged objections against these developments as part of the public participation process, and in return, Century brought a massive R197 million damages suit against GEKCO and its chair, Kristin Kallesen, in her personal capacity. Century claimed this was the cost of the delays that GEKCO's objections had caused. But legal experts and activists said this was not a legitimate case, but a SLAPP suit. SLAPP, or Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation, is a worrying growing trend globally: big corporates abusing court process and leveraging their greater resources to silence and intimidate communities, activists and journalists. But in the wake of a series of positive developments in South African law, Century has agreed to withdraw its claim against GEKCO. Activists hope it will mark a landmark in the battle against SLAPP in South Africa.

Script:


VOICEOVER: A defence of vital economic development?
UPSOUND: MARK CORBETT (CARTE BLANCHE 2021) You must understand that significant damage is done with their objections.
VOICEOVER: …or corporate bullying…?
UPSOUND: KRISTIN KALLESEN (CARTE BLANCHE 2021) They're asking for two hundred million rand, none of which any of us have.
VOICEOVER: What’s been called the biggest SLAPP suit in South African history has now been withdrawn. In February 2021, Century Property Developments brought a punishing R197 million suit against the Greater Kyalami Conservancy (GEKCO) and its chair, Kristin Kallesen.
UPSOUND: KRISTIN KALLESEN (CARTE BLANCHE 2021) It basically sues me in my personal capacity as well as the conservancy to reclaim alleged damages for delays due to the objections that were lodged during the public participation process.
VOICEOVER: GEKCO objected to developments north of Johannesburg, which it said encroached on sensitive wetlands.
UPSOUND: MARK CORBETT (CARTE BLANCHE 2021) This is the subject of the court case. This is Riversands…
VOICEOVER: Century, owned by property mogul Mark Corbett, claimed that GEKCO’s objections caused years of costly delays.
UPSOUND: MARK CORBETT (CARTE BLANCHE 2021) The figure of 197 million is very symbolic because that is the value of the economic activity that's been removed in this area. Riversands at present is only about 15 percent developed. But if it wasn't for GEKCO imagine where we would be. You know, I think it would be close to 70, 80 percent developed.
VOICEOVER: But GEKCO and its supporters saw the case as an attempt to intimidate and undermine: in other words, Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation, or SLAPP.
UPSOUND: LEANNE GOVINDSAMY: This was a SLAPP suit because it was what the Constitutional Court has referred to as an abuse of process. Any corporation may go to court to defend its good name, its reputation, but it becomes an abuse of process when it is done in order to suppress or intimidate activists. There's an inequality of arms if you could call it that. It is not done to vindicate rights.
VOICEOVER: GEKCO approached Asina Loyiko, an anti-SLAPP advocacy campaign. Leanne Govindsamy spoke to us on the movement’s behalf.
UPSOUND: LEANNE GOVINDSAMY: You need expert legal defence. You also need to pay attention to the kind of emotional distress that this kind of matter causes. Um, and quite importantly, how do you ensure that the essential work that they were doing at GEKCO could continue?
VOICEOVER: For more than three years, Century did nothing to pursue the suit.
UPSOUND: LEANNE GOVINDSAMY: The longer you drag a defendant through court, the more costs are incurred by those defendants and you prevent them from doing the essential work that they may be doing as activists in a community.
VOICEOVER: Meanwhile, in a separate case 2 years ago, the Constitutional Court handed down a landmark judgement outlining the elements of a SLAPP suit. Finally, last month, Century agreed to withdraw its claim.
UPSOUND: KRISTIN KALLESEN: It really feels fantastic. It's wonderful to know that that's not hanging over my head. And our head as the conservancy. And we hope that people will think twice before suing us or other environmental organisations in the future.
VOICEOVER: Mark Corbett told us GEKCO lodged an application seeking to have all Century’s approved developments declared invalid. When GEKCO withdrew that case, Century withdrew its damages claim as a show of good faith. But GEKCO insists the application sought recognition from the City of Johannesburg that GEKCO has the right to object to development applications. It was settled last January when the City confirmed GEKCO’s legal standing.
UPSOUND: LEANNE GOVINDSAMY: Even though the developments were allowed to go ahead, it's also important to recognize that the parallel legal process which resulted in GEKCO challenging the City of Johannesburg was also really important for public participation processes.
UPSOUND: KRISTIN KALLESEN: Unfortunately, the developments have had the impacts that we were concerned about. We have seen that some of the wetlands have been impacted.
VOICEOVER: Century says its developments are “real-world examples of inclusive economic growth” that protect the wetlands better than the conservancy does. It accuses GEKCO of opposing all development to preserve an elitist lifestyle. But GEKCO believes its mission has been validated.
UPSOUND: KRISTIN KALLESEN: We believe that the intent of the SLAPP suit was to prevent us from objecting and using our voice going forward in future applications, which we've continued to do. And the city has reduced densities and made some amendments that we were asking for. And so we are continuing to use our voice to ensure that the protection of the Kyalami area takes place.
UPSOUND: LEANNE GOVINDSAMY: This is a fundamental right that you're talking about. This is entrenched in our constitution. This is the point of having a public process.
